title: Oh No, Snakes!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore snakes in general: their roughly 2,700 species, why humans fear them and why indiscriminate killing is wrong, and how snakes sense the world (hearing through skull bones, vision, tongue-based smell via Jacobson's organ). They cover snake breathing and lungs, shedding skin (molting), indeterminate growth, the four main modes of locomotion (serpentine, sidewinding, caterpillar, concertina), large snakes including anacondas and the fossil Titanoboa, feeding and jaw unhinging, venom and venomous fangs, constriction, snake mating and reproduction, a ranking of the world's most venomous snakes, and the myth of snakes in Ireland. The episode closes with a listener mail from Kristen about how the show helped her through lupus-related depression and panic attacks.

segments.title: Opening banter and snake fear
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter, then introduce the episode and discuss how snakes are needlessly killed out of fear, and the evolutionary basis of human snake detection.

segments.title: Snake basics and senses
segments.summary: Snakes number about 2,700 species, have no limbs, are carnivorous and ectothermic. They hear through vibrations in skull bones, have limited color vision with good vision above ground, and smell by flicking the tongue to Jacobson's organs.

segments.title: Snake breathing and digestion
segments.summary: Snake digestive tract runs the length of the body. Many have one lung, and their oxygen consumption rises while digesting large prey. They breathe by expanding and contracting their ribs and can extend a breathing tube out of the mouth while swallowing prey.

segments.title: Shedding skin and indeterminate growth
segments.summary: Snakes shed their whole outer skin by molting, with scales made of keratin, a liquefied layer separating old and new skin, and rubbing against rocks to peel it off. Molting takes about two weeks and snakes keep growing throughout life.

segments.title: Snake locomotion
segments.summary: Snakes move via vertebrae and ventral scales. The four main methods are serpentine (undulatory), sidewinding (on sand), caterpillar (rectilinear), and concertina (used for climbing). Swimming snakes move quickly in water.

segments.title: Anacondas and the Titanoboa
segments.summary: Anacondas are large swimming constrictors in South American rivers that can hold their breath for up to ten minutes. The Titanoboa, a fossil snake about 56 million years old found in a Colombian coal pit, grew to about 40 feet and a ton, with a rare intact skull.

segments.title: Feeding, jaw unhinging, and venom
segments.summary: Snakes swallow prey whole by unhinging their jaws via the quadrate bone, and backward-curving teeth help move prey down. Venomous snakes have hollow fangs and venom glands; venom contains neurotoxins, cardiotoxins, hemotoxins, and anticoagulants. Some snakes are poisonous rather than venomous by storing toxins from prey.

segments.title: Constriction and a personal encounter
segments.summary: Boas and anacondas kill by constriction, squeezing so the heart and lungs cannot function. The hosts share personal snake encounters, including a host holding a boa and a childhood rattlesnake encounter in North Georgia.

segments.title: Snake mating and reproduction
segments.summary: Female snakes release pheromones that males follow. The male bumps her head with his chin before the pair intertwine tails and cloacae meet so the male delivers sperm through his hemipenes. Snakes may lay eggs, bear live young (one to 150), or do both; some protect eggs or leave them.

segments.title: Most venomous snakes and snakes in Ireland
segments.summary: A ranking of the world's most venomous snakes is discussed, including the Eastern diamondback, death adder, viper, Philippine cobra, tiger snake, black mamba, taipan, blue krait, Eastern brown snake and inland taipan. The hosts also discuss the myth that St. Patrick drove snakes from Ireland and the Everglades python problem.
